prize_parts.citation: for discoveries on the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and for the mechanism-based design of long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonists that established incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: a single prize part on B025 to Drucker, Holst and Knudsen. Round 1 showed that the six of us agree on the achievement and differ only on one seat, so the remaining question is what the prize is for. The change in the field is not the hormone alone. Proglucagon processing, the incretin effect and the insulinotropic and satiety actions of GLP-1 (Holst, Drucker) explained a mechanism, but native GLP-1 is degraded within minutes by DPP-4 and cleared rapidly, so it could not be a medicine. Solving that specific biological problem through fatty-acid acylation, albumin binding and resistance to degradation (Knudsen) is what produced once-daily and once-weekly agonists and the outcome-trial evidence on glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal disease. Without that step the physiology would not have altered medicine in the way the prize requires. Maturity is not in doubt after decades of replication and more than a decade of clinical use. The chair's point that the analogue work carried real mechanistic content, and not only industrial optimisation, has moved me to word the citation so that both the physiology and the design of the long-acting agonists are named explicitly. The configuration is then defensible whichever way the committee frames the prize.
statement.case_against: The attribution problem has not been resolved by the exchange. Mojsov's identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is a discovery-stage contribution, her role is credited on the shortlist and three colleagues name her, and Habener is outside the credited names, so any trio excludes someone with a defensible claim. Knudsen's work was done in a company, and if the committee holds that the prize should reward physiology alone, then my trio is the wrong one and Drucker, Holst and Mojsov would be more consistent. I have not seen evidence in the supplied material that settles Mojsov's priority against Habener, and I will not claim that I can adjudicate it from recollection. A further concern is that unanimity at the opening ballot, and a single-part prize, mean the second tier (CAR-T, the unfolded protein response, optogenetics) is not recognised this year, and that is a real cost even if I think combining any of them with B025 would reduce the GLP-1 trio below a defensible size.

responses.point: Linnarsson argues that if Mojsov's role is uncertain, the committee should scrutinise the record on who first established the active GLP-1(7-36) form and its insulinotropic action, rather than substitute someone from a different category of contribution.
responses.response: That is a fair challenge and I agree that the scrutiny should come before the vote. My position on it is conditional. If the supplied record showed that Mojsov established the active form and its insulinotropic action independently and first, I would treat her seat as a physiology seat and compare her with Knudsen on the same footing. The record we have does not show that, and the credit text itself describes the priority as disputed with someone we cannot name. A prize should not rest on a seat whose basis the committee cannot defend. I also do not accept that Knudsen belongs to a different category. Designing an albumin-binding, DPP-4-resistant analogue answered a defined biological question about half-life, and that is a mechanistic contribution on the path to the discovery being useful. I am therefore not persuaded to move unless the priority evidence is clearly in Mojsov's favour.

responses.point: El-Manira keeps Mojsov over Knudsen because the prize should reward discovery of the active peptide and the biology, and not the optimisation of a molecule, much of it done in industry. He accepts that this is a judgement about which of two real contributions to omit.
responses.response: I agree with your last sentence and it is where we actually stand: two real contributions, one seat, and no scientific fact that separates them. I differ on the word optimisation. Moving from a native peptide with a half-life of minutes to an agent given weekly was not a refinement of a known drug; it determined whether incretin biology reached patients at all. The ordering also matters for credibility, because a physiology-only citation will be read against the semaglutide and liraglutide data that the public already associates with this prize. I do not claim the industrial setting is irrelevant, only that the committee has honoured work done in industry where the discovery was the step that mattered. If you and the others decide that physiology alone is the remit, I would regard Drucker, Holst and Mojsov as a legitimate outcome and not a mistaken one.

responses.point: Svenningsson agrees with the trio, says that calling the analogue work development alone understates how much of it was mechanistic (half-life, albumin binding, DPP-4 resistance), and proposes that the citation name both the physiology and the development explicitly so that it is defensible either way.
responses.response: I accept the correction to how I described the analogue work in round 1. Treating it as development alone was too coarse, and I have rewritten my citation to name both parts, as you suggest. I would add one caution to your proposal. A citation that names both physiology and therapy will only protect us if the three names fit it cleanly. Here Drucker and Holst carry the physiology, Knudsen carries the design, and nobody in the trio carries the identification of the active peptide. That omission is visible, and the citation cannot hide it. The honest position is that the committee chooses the long-acting-agonist framing knowingly, with Mojsov and Habener acknowledged in the background of the prize and not in the citation.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius keeps Knudsen because the prize category has repeatedly honoured the step that turns a mechanism into a medicine, and would accept the Mojsov variant only if the committee settles the priority question. She keeps B047 and B014 as alternatives and ranks B014 above B038.
responses.response: I agree with the principle you state and with the conditional you attach to Mojsov, which is the same one I hold. Where I would be slightly more careful is the argument from tradition. Precedent supports recognising a translational step, but it does not by itself decide that this step is a discovery, so I rest the case on the mechanistic content of the acylation strategy and not on previous prizes. On B014 I note your argument that it has population-level effect on cancer prevention, and I treat it as a serious alternative on evidence. I still keep it out of my own alternatives because of the attribution record (Zhou's early death, parallel groups, patent-shaped priority) and the proximity to the 2008 HPV prize, and I keep B047 and B051 ahead of it for that reason.

responses.point: Sandberg keeps Drucker, Holst and Mojsov because identifying GLP-1(7-36) as the active form is a discovery-level step on which later pharmacology depended, whereas Knudsen's design is development. He says he would move if the committee shows Mojsov's priority cannot be defended, and he would give Knudsen more weight under a translation-oriented citation.
responses.response: This is the clearest statement of the conditional that decides our disagreement, and I think we agree on its structure. You would move toward Knudsen if Mojsov's priority fails, and I would move toward Mojsov if it holds and the committee wants a physiology-only prize. Neither of us can test that from the material supplied. I do disagree that the later pharmacology depended on identification of the active form in the same sense it depended on the incretin physiology and on the problem of degradation, since the drug-design step needed the knowledge of what DPP-4 does to the peptide, which is Drucker's and Holst's contribution. I also agree with you that a second prize part would shrink the GLP-1 trio below a defensible size, which is why I stay with a single part and treat B047 only as an alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee frames B025 as physiology only or as physiology plus mechanism-based design of long-acting agonists; this alone decides between Knudsen and Mojsov for the third seat, and I cannot verify Mojsov's priority against Habener from the supplied record.
Whether Habener's absence from the credited names makes every B025 configuration open to the charge of rewriting history, including my own.
Whether the acylation and albumin-binding work is accepted as a discovery in its own right and not as industrial development.
Whether a second prize part (B047 or B051) could be justified without reducing the B025 trio, given the three-person limit and the attribution gap on Eshhar for CAR-T.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my round 1 disclosure. No shortlisted credited name is a person with whom my profile records a relationship. My profile records past co-authorship with Ronald Evans, whose work is outside the shortlist, and collaborations with Johan Ericson, Per Svenningsson and Abdel El Manira. Svenningsson and El Manira are committee colleagues and not credited names, so no recusal is required. My nuclear-receptor and dopamine-neuron work does not overlap with any shortlisted discovery.
